text: A hands-on pass through the two pieces of classical coding theory this chapter has used — success-probability arithmetic and minimum distance — before this course moves fully into the quantum case.

Here's the same success-probability calculation from before, carried out for a new channel flip rate, p equals 0.08, across repetition codes of length 1, 3, 5, and 7. An uncoded bit succeeds 92% of the time; the 3-bit code, 98.1824%; the 5-bit code, 99.5475%; the 7-bit code, 99.8824%. The pattern holds: going from n=1 to n=3 cuts the failure rate from 8% down to about 1.8%, while going from n=5 to n=7 only cuts it from about 0.45% down to about 0.12% — a smaller absolute gain, because there's less failure left to remove.

A code's minimum distance is the smallest number of positions in which any two valid codewords differ. For the 3-bit repetition code, the only two codewords, 000 and 111, differ in all 3 positions, so its minimum distance is 3. The general rule: a code with minimum distance d can detect up to d minus 1 errors, and correct up to the floor of d minus 1 over 2. Plug in d equals 3: it detects up to 2 errors and corrects exactly 1 — matching the 3-bit code precisely. The 5-bit code has minimum distance 5, giving 2 correctable errors, again matching its success-probability math.

This distance-to-correction-power relationship, d greater than or equal to 2t plus 1 to correct t errors, is not a classical-only fact — it reappears unchanged in form for every quantum code in this course. The Steane code in Chapter 4 is called a 7-1-3 code specifically because its minimum distance is 3, which is exactly why, like the 3-bit repetition code, it corrects exactly 1 arbitrary single-qubit error, no more.

Carrying this one relationship forward is the single most useful thing to take out of this classical review chapter. Next, Chapter 3 builds the first real quantum error-correcting code from everything established here: the three-qubit bit-flip code.
